extracted.intended_audience: researchers, practitioners, policymakers and general readers interested in designing or evaluating crowdsourcing projects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative considerations for running or assessing crowdsourcing initiatives (microtasks, citizen science, crowdfunding, translation, etc.), focusing on data quality, participant selection, incentives, labor/ethical issues, and platform design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality / verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Susceptibility to faulty results caused by targeted/malicious work or workers rushing because they are paid per task; verifying responses is time-consuming and often requires multiple workers per task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect trade-offs: redundancy (having multiple workers do the same task) increases accuracy but also time and monetary costs. Use vetting of crowdworkers (e.g., repeated vetting as done by some companies) to control quality. Plan for verification overhead and balance cost vs required accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task design (classes vs free-form & granularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling crowdsourcing tasks as fixed classes/options can unnecessarily restrict quality; participants provide more accurate information when classifying at a more general level, and overall accuracy can be greater when free-form responses are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks to allow appropriate granularity (not overly constrained classes) and consider including open-ended responses. In behavioral research, include open-ended responses plus attention checks to assess data quality. Beware that more general classifications may be less actionable for sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker skill and expertise fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds lack sufficient skills/expertise for complex tasks (e.g., engineering design, product validation); anonymous online crowds often perform worse than experts on complex evaluations like business-model assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crowdsourcing for 'simple' tasks (e.g., image labeling) or 'intermediate' tasks only if you can estimate worker skills/intentions and apply inference methods (which may add computational cost). For complex tasks, recruit domain experts rather than relying exclusively on anonymous crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and sampling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdworkers constitute a non-random, biased sample of the population: participation skews by country development level (low in low- and high-developed countries, higher in medium-developed countries), and participants sometimes masquerade as being from other locales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate demographic and geographic biases when generalizing results; implement screening and validation to reduce misrepresentation (e.g., location verification). Consider how platform access and pay levels shape your sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives, motivation, and completion/attrition rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of sufficient monetary motivation or too few participants increases the likelihood of project failure; tasks not completed quickly may be forgotten (long-tail completion distribution); low-paying studies have higher attrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incentive structures and timelines to reduce attrition and speed up completion. Monitor task visibility and reward levels to avoid long-tail delays and high dropout rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client–worker interaction and product knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of interaction between crowd and client — little information about the final product and rare worker–client interaction — can decrease product quality because client interaction is vital to design processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where product quality matters, incorporate mechanisms for client feedback, iterative interaction, or clearer briefs so workers understand context and intended outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration tools and knowledge-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd-workers often lack collaboration tools and organizational structures typical in workplaces (shared procedures, information, tools), which impedes building on each other's knowledge and reduces product quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide collaboration platforms, shared documentation, and tooling where tasks require coordination or cumulative knowledge. Avoid designs that isolate workers when teamwork would improve outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor concentration and authorship distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourced projects are expected to be unbiased by many diverse contributors, but often a small number of people (or a single person) produce the majority of the output while the crowd contributes minor details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contribution distributions and be cautious about claims of 'crowd-created' outputs. Implement metrics/visibility for individual contributions if equitable recognition or distributed authorship is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital-raising and investor dynamics in crowdfunding
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing/crowdfunding simplifies access to capital by many smaller investors, speeding project starts; however, many small, risk-seeking investors can reduce entrepreneurs' experience persuading cautious investors and can change risk assessment incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade-offs: easier capital vs. potential loss of governance, mentorship, and rigorous vetting that larger institutional investors provide. Plan governance and investor engagement accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker classification, compensation, and labor rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdworkers are typically classified as independent contractors and are not guaranteed minimum wage; low reported hourly earnings on platforms (e.g., MTurk) have raised ethical concerns and calls for organizing for labor rights. Typically there are no written employment contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical implications of pay and classification; consider fair-pay policies, transparent terms, and dispute/appeal mechanisms. Be aware requesters can withhold pay and that this practice raises exploitation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform incentives for or against worker collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Some crowdsourcing models discourage collaboration (especially competitive crowdsourcing) resulting in low teamwork rates; platform design can limit or enable worker collaboration and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If collective problem-solving benefits the task, choose or design platforms that permit/teamwork and sharing. Monitor whether competition vs. collaboration is appropriate for your goals (e.g., InnoCentive reports low team submissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/contractual protections and payment withholding
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical absence of written contracts, nondisclosure or employee agreements means employers decide acceptability of work and may reserve the right to withhold pay (e.g., MTurk requesters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify terms of payment and acceptance up-front; include fair dispute resolution and transparent acceptance criteria to avoid withholding and litigation risks. Consider whether formal agreements are necessary for sensitive or high-value work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical, privacy and mental-health risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns include privacy violations, hiring vulnerable groups, breaches of anonymity, psychological damage, encouragement of addictive behaviors, and overlap with content-moderation harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and mitigate ethical risks: ensure informed consent, protect anonymity, avoid exploitative recruitment of vulnerable groups, provide mental-health support where necessary, and comply with privacy regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for machine-learning dataset collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing is widely used to collect large human-labeled datasets (images, text) for training ML models, but quality and representativeness issues affect resulting model performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using crowdsourcing for ML data, implement robust quality checks (gold standards, redundancy, vetting), labeler training, and sampling strategies to ensure dataset quality and reduce biases that will propagate into models.
